title: Cache-aside
summary: Cache-aside lets application code reuse a stored result, then fetch and cache missing data. A hit proves presence, not freshness.
overview: The application owns the lookup, source read, and cache fill. An update path can commit to the source and then delete the cached entry. These operations are separate: another writer, a failed deletion, or an overlapping reader can leave outdated data available. This chapter concerns exact-key data caching behind an agent tool, not model prompt caching or similarity-based answer reuse.
why: Use this when repeated tool reads create measurable source load. Delegation makes a stale result consequential: an agent may use an old runbook to propose a deployment. First decide which decisions tolerate old information; adding a cache is not a prerequisite for adopting agents.
example: Illustrative scenario: a release-planning agent calls readRunbook(team, service). The cached guide is revision 1. An editor publishes revision 2 with a changed rollback step, but misses invalidation. The tool returns revision 1 again. A recovery operation deletes the key; the following lookup fetches revision 2 and caches it. No deployment executes in this example.
judgment: Start with measured repeated reads and an explicit freshness budget. Treat five minutes as a test setting, not a recommendation. Choose keys for the result’s full scope, and keep authorization in application code on every request, including hits. Persistent instructions cannot enforce permissions. Decide whether a failed fresh read should block the proposed action.
next: Can you pause a reader after it fetches revision 1, commit revision 2 and invalidate, then resume the reader and observe revision 1 reappear?

learning.relevance: Engineers building agent tools need this when repeated retrieval makes source capacity or latency a practical problem. Keep it as a supporting chapter because most teams should establish trustworthy tool results and review boundaries before optimizing retrieval.
outcomes: Trace a hit and a miss, identifying which component reads the source and populates the cache.
Reproduce a stale fill after invalidation with a controlled concurrent reader.
Specify key scope, freshness checks, and source-load limits for one tool.

workflow.before: An engineer opens the authoritative runbook, checks its revision, and writes a release plan for review.
workflow.after: An agent requests the runbook through a tool that returns its source revision and retrieval time, then drafts the plan with those references.
workflow.human: The engineer owns access rules, the acceptable freshness budget, and approval of the proposed operational steps.

walkthrough: 1. Define the contract. Use a mock runbook containing revision and rollbackStep. For this exercise, key the result by team, service, and output-schema version. The team and service come from validated request context; knowing a key never grants access.

2. Implement the read path. After authorization, look up the key. On a miss, read the source and cache the returned object. For Redis, SET key value EX 300 attaches expiration in the same command. EXPIRE sets a key’s timeout; Redis removes the key after that timeout expires, and a plain GET does not renew its timeout. Cache lifetime is not proof of source freshness.

3. Implement the update path. Record a successful source commit before deleting the key. Surface deletion failures for recovery. Return the source revision to the caller so a reviewer can compare it against the authoritative revision before relying on operational instructions.

4. Challenge the happy path. Pause an in-flight old read until after deletion, then release it. A version label alone cannot prevent stale refill. For an action requiring current instructions, make an authoritative recheck part of its execution contract and define what happens if that check fails. A check establishes freshness only at the time it reads the authority; if a later action requires the same revision, the execution system must enforce that revision precondition or revalidate under an appropriate concurrency contract.
pitfalls: Caching a permission decision alongside content and reusing it after access changes: check authorization for every tool call.
Treating expiration as a consistency guarantee: an old in-flight read can populate a newly expiring entry after a write.
Letting simultaneous misses or a cache outage flood the source: test with caching disabled, coalesce duplicate work where appropriate, and cap downstream concurrency.

exercise.title: Make a stale runbook visible
steps: Build an in-memory source and cache with a controllable pause between source read and cache fill.
Perform one cold read followed by two warm reads and record source-read counts; change the source without deletion and observe the old revision.
Delete the key and read again, checking that the new revision appears.
Run the paused-reader race and capture the stale result; add an authoritative revision check before accepting the plan.
success: An initial cold read followed by two warm reads produces exactly one source fetch; deletion causes the next read to fetch again.
The race is reproducible, and the acceptance check rejects a plan whose cited revision differs from the current source.
